title: Grand Jury Declines Charges in Death of College Football Player Nolan Wells
snippet: A Mississippi grand jury concluded that no criminal charges are warranted in the tragic drowning death of 18-year-old Nolan Wells.
content:
A Jackson County grand jury has formally declined to bring criminal charges in the tragic death of 18-year-old Nolan Wells, concluding a high-profile inquiry into the college football player's drowning off the coast of Mississippi this summer.

According to a detailed report released late Monday night, the 23-member grand jury determined that the evidence surrounding the position, condition, and location of Wells' body off Horn Island is entirely consistent with an accidental drowning. The panel found no credible evidence indicating foul play or criminal conduct by anyone accompanying Wells on the water.

Evidence Points to Accidental Drowning

Wells vanished on July 4, 2026, while celebrating the holiday with friends on barrier islands along the Gulf Coast. His body was recovered two days later. The grand jury heard testimony from 43 witnesses and reviewed extensive physical evidence, digital records, police reports, and autopsy findings.

While decomposition made toxicology results somewhat inconclusive, tests revealed no cocaine in Wells' system. Investigators noted that Wells had purchased alcohol using a fake ID prior to the trip. Though a minor bruise was discovered on the back of his head, medical examiners confirmed it was not a fatal injury. One witness testified under oath to seeing Wells slip awkwardly off the side of a boat around the time he was last seen, though he continued socializing afterward without showing signs of injury.

Addressing Online Speculation

The grand jury report directly addressed the intense national attention and widespread online speculation that plagued the investigation. Unfounded accusations and threats had targeted Wells' friends and their families, particularly regarding why Wells' cell phone was brought back to the mainland on a different vessel.

The report clarified that exchanging items or returning on different boats is common during island gatherings, noting that Wells' phone was not the only one brought back without its owner. The panel forcefully dismissed the public attacks against the boaters as malicious, false, and devoid of factual support.

Attorneys representing the Wells family conducted a separate private investigation and similarly advised that they found no evidence of criminal activity. While the grand jury's findings clear all parties involved for now, officials noted that Mississippi has no statute of limitations on homicide, leaving the door open to review any new credible evidence that may surface in the future.
